book_title: Life Breaks In: A Mood Almanack
subject_line: Cloud-writing and the moods of Life Breaks In
email_body:
Dear Mary,

Life Breaks In takes its title from a Virginia Woolf line and treats mood almost as weather, something you approach through what you call cloud-writing rather than argument. Your later Lecture, written for Transit Books' Undelivered Lecture Series, seems to push that same restlessness about form in another direction. I'd love to ask how you decide when a subject needs an almanack, a lecture or an essay, and what training first as a poet still gives your prose.

subject_line: From Cut Off the Ears of Winter to The Right Place to Jump
email_body:
Dear Peter,

The PEN/Osterweil judges described Cut Off the Ears of Winter as elegant and disturbing, poems that look at childhood abuse and the brutality under ordinary events. Your later New Issues collection, The Right Place to Jump, arrives years after that first book, and I'm curious what changed in how you approach difficult material over that stretch, and how teaching creative writing at the University of Rhode Island has shaped your sense of what a poem owes its reader.

subject_line: Fighting as "The Stone" in Roughhouse Friday
email_body:
Dear Jaed,

Roughhouse Friday takes its title from the barroom fight night in Juneau, and I was struck that you told InsideHook the project began as journalism before it became a memoir, and that you never told anyone back East you had fought. I'd love to ask what made you move from reporting on the ring to writing yourself into it as "The Stone," and how teaching fiction and nonfiction in UNH's MFA program has changed how you think about turning lived experience into story.

book_title: Punch Me Up to the Gods
subject_line: "We Real Cool" as the skeleton of Punch Me Up to the Gods
email_body:
Dear Brian,

You've said that when you read Gwendolyn Brooks's "We Real Cool" you saw a small treatise on Black masculinity, and that the poem ended up deciding the structure of Punch Me Up to the Gods, with its jumping timelines. I'd love to ask what it was like to let someone else's eight lines govern a memoir, and whether that habit of borrowing form from poetry has carried into what you're writing and teaching now at West Virginia University.

subject_line: After Air, Light, Dust, Shadow, Distance: The Return from Calvary
email_body:
Dear Mary Ann,

AGNI once described your poems in Beauty Breaks In as mixing a sly, strained wit with a meditative urge, and that pairing seems to run through Air, Light, Dust, Shadow, Distance, which won the 42 Miles Press Poetry Award. With The Return from Calvary now out and read at WVU this spring, I'd love to ask how that meditative habit sits alongside a title so charged with religious weight, and what the new book asked of you that the earlier ones didn't.

subject_line: Karl Hofer's painting and the sequence of Early Hour
email_body:
Dear Michael,

Early Hour is built as a single book-length sequence answering Karl Hofer's 1935 painting of the same name, which feels like a long way from the catalogue of mills, sloughs and industry in your poem "Coos Bay" from Choke. I'd love to ask how a German Expressionist canvas became the frame for a whole book, whether the Oregon coast still finds its way in, and how directing the MFA program at the University of Idaho fits around your own writing.

subject_line: Fatherhood and moving water in The River You Touch
email_body:
Dear Chris,

The River You Touch turns from the bonefish guide of Body of Water to your own household, with your wife and children woven through a life spent guiding on western Montana rivers. You came to Missoula at nineteen because of Norman Maclean, and I'd love to ask how it feels to now be writing a river memoir in his shadow, and how moving between poems like Ragged Anthem and long-form prose changes the way you look at the same water.

subject_line: From Milledgeville to Montana, after Dangerous Goods
email_body:
Dear Sean,

Blood Ties & Brown Liquor grew out of Milledgeville, and you talked through its sources with Natasha Trethewey on the porch of Flannery O'Connor's Andalusia; Dangerous Goods then won the Minnesota Book Award while you were in Bemidji. Now that you are teaching at the University of Montana, I'd love to ask how each new landscape has altered the voices you let into your poems, and what the West is asking of your work that Georgia and Minnesota did not.

subject_line: Writing past sadness in Love Prodigal
email_body:
Dear Traci,

At your Ulrich Museum reading you told The Sunflower that sadness is a much easier emotion for you to write, and that it took until a fourth book to attempt the other kind; Love Prodigal, your Copper Canyon collection, reads as that attempt. After Come the Slumberless to the Land of Nod, I'd love to ask what it took to stay with tenderness on the page without flinching, and how serving as Kansas Poet Laureate has shaped who you imagine reading these poems.

I'd love to ask how a private ethic of attention stretches to hold something as large as a crisis, and how working as Poet in Residence at the University of Maryland has fed that shift.

subject_line: Debt, love and generated lines in Negative Money
email_body:
Dear Lillian-Yvonne,

Negative Money moves through race, gender, debt and love in a range of forms, and you've described computational poetry as writing programs that generate words and lines within set parameters. Your chapbook A Black Story May Contain Sensitive Content has since been read in Callaloo alongside Mary Prince. I'd love to ask where you draw the line between what the machine produces and what you claim as the poem, and how directing UMD's creative writing program shapes that thinking.

subject_line: A plate-lunch family and a ghost at the DMZ
email_body:
Dear Joseph,

Nuclear Family begins with the Cho family's Korean plate-lunch business in Hawaiʻi faltering after a viral video of Jacob trying to cross the DMZ, his family unaware he carries his grandfather's ghost. You told Ploughshares that fiction became a place to learn for yourself what your family had endured, and you set concrete-poetry interludes in the middle of the novel. I'd love to ask how those visual pages came about, and how teaching novel craft at UH Mānoa feeds your writing.

subject_line: Photons, exoplanets and airborne poison in Vapor
email_body:
Dear Sara,

Vapor moves between the body and the cosmos, from photons and black holes to blood, and the Anchorage Daily News read its title sequence as poems about death by airborne poison. Reviewers have also noticed how it carries over the spare world-building of Bone Map. I'd love to ask how scientific language entered your poems, whether living and teaching in Fairbanks shapes that sense of scale, and what you are drawn to writing after this second book.

book_title: Made in China: A Memoir of Love and Labor
subject_line: The garment shop and the report in Made in China
email_body:
Dear Anna,

Made in China turns on a teenager sent to work in her family's garment shop in Queens and treated as a maid at home, and on the child welfare report she makes that later resurfaces with the wrong details. I'd love to ask how you approached writing about your mother without flattening her, what it meant to set your own account against that official file, and how teaching at the University of Wyoming has changed how you think about memoir.

subject_line: Horoscopes, tarot and grief in Daughter in Retrograde
email_body:
Dear Courtney,

Daughter in Retrograde follows your mother Victoria's final years through horoscopes and other tools of divination, set against Eau Claire's townie culture, and you sat for your interview in The Common only after a tarot reading. You've called her death the defining moment of your life. I'd love to ask how astrology gave you a structure for writing grief that ordinary chronology couldn't, and how teaching creative nonfiction at the University of North Dakota has shaped what you're working on now.
